note: Editorial: the reference (Pakistan IKMC) copy prints the name as "Franois" (the c-cedilla was lost in typesetting); restored to "François".
Choices (A)–(D) are pictures and choice (E) is text; the figure shows the cube and the four picture choices.
The question asks for $x$, while the figure labels the vertex with a capital X.
The choices are printed without degree signs in the reference paper; kept as printed.
Editorial correction: the Pakistan IKMC paper prints choice (B) as "$3\sqrt{2} : x$" (a font error for $\pi$); $3\sqrt{2} : \pi$ is restored as in the Austrian English version of the same problem.

Source substitution in the reference: the Pakistan IKMC 2016 paper has a national question 29 (remainders of $(n+1)^3$ divided by $n^3$). The KSF question 29 (this chessboard problem) is taken from the Cyprus paper, which agrees with the Austrian English version of the same problem.

Source ambiguity: the national English/translated copies of this KSF problem differ in the choices: Canada (used here) prints 11, 7, 8, 9, 10; Austria prints 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 (both with 12 cubes and the same 12-cube drawing). Cyprus prints a 10-cube variant with choices 6–10.

Editorial: the two crossing types are separate small pictures inside the sentence ('like this: [picture] or like this: [picture]'); they are reproduced side by side below the knot in the figure, and the bracketed references were added to the text.

Name: the Saudi Mawhiba booklet localises the name ('Hashem'); the KSF name Henry is used (as in the Cyprus paper). The Pakistan IKMC 2022 paper replaces this question with a national problem, so the Saudi booklet is the reference for Q1.

Source ambiguity: choice (E) is "none of the previous" in the Saudi Mawhiba copy (also Cyprus; Austria "another number"), but "42" in the Swedish NCM English copy of the KSF paper. The Saudi reading is kept.

Source ambiguity: choice (E) is printed $\frac{\pi}{3r}$ in the Saudi Mawhiba copy but $\frac{\pi}{2r}$ in the Swedish NCM and Austrian English copies and in Cyprus; the majority reading $\frac{\pi}{2r}$ is given.

Source ambiguity: choice (E) is "none of the previous" in the Saudi Mawhiba copy (also Cyprus; Austria "an other number"), but $2^4 \cdot 3^6$ in the Swedish NCM English copy. The Saudi reading is kept.

Source ambiguity: the Saudi Mawhiba copy prints choice (E) as "none-negative" (Arabic: non-negative), whereas the Swedish NCM ("None of the other options are true"), Austrian ("None of these four statements is definitely true") and Cyprus copies have "none of the others is always true"; the majority reading is given.
The Austrian national version of this problem uses underwear instead of socks and different choices (A) €6.00 and (E) €8.40; the Swedish English version agrees with the Cyprus choices.

Editorial correction: the Cyprus paper (English and Greek lines) prints the condition as "α = (b/c)²" with a Greek alpha; the digit $a$ of $\overline{abc}$ is meant, as in the Austrian and Swedish English versions of the same problem.
Editorial: the Cyprus English text names the first point with a Greek alpha ("points α, b, c and d"); the figure labels it $a$, as do the Greek line of the same paper and the Swedish English version.
The Swedish English version agrees with Cyprus (points on the edges of a cube); the Austrian national version places the nine points on the axes of a 3D coordinate system.
Editorial: the Cyprus paper defines $a_n$ but writes the sum with Greek alphas ("α1 − α2 + … + α2025 − α2026"); the Latin $a_n$ is used throughout, as in the Austrian and Swedish English versions.
Editorial correction: the reference paper prints "an an isoceles triangle"; the doubled article and the spelling are corrected.

Source ambiguity: the Pakistan IKMC Junior paper prints a four-piece variant (a $4\times2\times2$ cuboid made of four pieces, the same problem as in the KSF Ecolier paper and the Pakistan Cadet paper). The Junior papers of Cyprus and Austria both print this three-piece version ($3\times2\times2$ cuboid, same five choice drawings), which is taken here as the KSF Junior problem; text and figure from the Cyprus paper.

Editorial correction: the reference paper's text says "The square $ABCE$ ... the distance from the point $D$ to the line $g$" and choice (E) "Depends on the location of $D$", which contradicts its own figure (square $ABCD$ with $E$ outside it) and the triangle $ECD$. The labels are corrected to the figure, as in the Austrian and Canadian versions (square $ABCD$, distance from $E$).

Source ambiguity: the Cyprus and Austria Junior papers print instead the computation problem "To the number 6 we add 3 ..." (also the KSF Benjamin/Cadet problem), while the Canadian grade 9-10 paper prints a variant of this replace-each-8 problem; the reference (Pakistan) problem is kept.

Source ambiguity: the order of the last two choices differs between national versions: the reference (Pakistan) paper prints (D) 60, (E) 50; the Cyprus paper (D) 50, (E) 60; the Canadian paper lists 60, 50, 40, 30, 20; the Austrian paper (D) 60% and (E) "too little information". The reference order is kept.
Editorial correction: the reference paper prints "bigger then"; corrected to "bigger than".
The reference paper (and the Cyprus paper) spells the third sister both "Hannah" and "Hanna"; kept as printed.

Source ambiguity: the reference paper adds the editorial remark "[Possible to take away first die on the picture!]" after the question; it is omitted here. The reference, Cyprus and Austrian papers show three dice, while the Canadian version shows the die in two positions.

Source ambiguity: the Pakistan paper prints a different problem as Q23 (shaded square in a 3 x 3 grid); this KSF Q23 follows the Cyprus paper, whose choices 11, 12, 13, 14, 15 agree with the Austrian paper; the Canadian version prints the choices 10, 12, 13, 14, 24.

Source ambiguity: the Pakistan and Canada Cadet papers print this four-piece version ($4\times2\times2$ cuboid, also the KSF Ecolier problem). Source ambiguity: the drawings of the solid and of the five views differ between the Cyprus, Austrian and Canadian papers; the Cyprus artwork is used.
